summary.text: In classical physics where movement is far slower than light, relative velocity is calculated by adding the individual speeds together.
Phrases referring to relative velocity describe an object's motion within a frame of reference where another object remains stationary.
Using classical velocity addition breaks special relativity because it wrongly claims observers measure varying speeds for light.

facts.label: Classical speed condition
facts.value: Much less than the speed of light

facts.label: Vector rotation impact
facts.value: No effect on relative speed magnitude

items.prompt: If a person walks forward at 10 km/h on top of a train moving at 40 km/h, what is their total speed relative to the ground under classical rules?

options.label: 50 km/h
30 km/h
40 km/h
10 km/h

items.explain: Classical relative velocity dictates adding the walking speed of 10 km/h to the train's speed of 40 km/h, giving 50 km/h after one hour.

items.prompt: Which of the following is a standard way to express 'the velocity of A relative to B'?

options.label: The speed of B measured when A has completely stopped moving
The velocity of A in a coordinate system where B is always at rest
The velocity of A multiplied by the speed of B
The distance between A and B divided by two hours

items.explain: A legitimate expression for the velocity of A relative to B is its velocity inside a system where B is held at rest.

items.prompt: Why does simple classical velocity addition fail under special relativity?

options.label: It causes moving objects to lose all forward momentum over time.
It assumes light travels much slower than physical objects like trains.
It falsely predicts that different observers measure different light speeds.
It makes walking on moving platforms mathematically impossible.

items.explain: The classical addition formula violates special relativity because it incorrectly claims observers measure different light speeds.

items.prompt: Classical or Newtonian approximations of relative motion only apply under which physical constraint?

options.label: The motion occurs strictly over a one-hour period.
The speeds are much faster than the speed of light.
The movement occurs strictly along parallel paths.
All involved speeds are much less than the speed of light.

items.explain: Newtonian relative motion starts with the approximation that all speeds are far below the speed of light.

items.prompt: What happens to a coordinate system when it undergoes two Lorentz transformations in succession?

options.label: The coordinate system rotates.
It expands into extra spatial dimensions.
Its overall velocity drops to zero.
It reverses the direction of relative speeds.

items.explain: Two successive Lorentz transformations result in a rotation of the coordinate system.

items.prompt: How does coordinate rotation from successive Lorentz transformations affect relative speed?

options.label: It doubles the relative speed between parallel objects.
It does not affect vector magnitude, keeping relative speed symmetrical.
It makes relative speed completely asymmetrical and unpredictable.
It reduces the vector magnitude to zero.

items.explain: Rotation has no effect on a vector's magnitude, which maintains the symmetry of relative speed.
